newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac issues warning as Socialists grow confident.
newsitem.headline: Chirac issues warning as Socialists grow confident.

text.p: Conservative President Jacques Chirac warned on Wednesday that changing direction could be risky for France as leftist leaders sounded increasingly confident of victory in a snap parliamentary election.

Stocks plunged by three percent in late morning trade on worries that the Socialist-Communist bloc would win Sunday's decisive runoff ballot. Bonds were off their highs but steady and the franc stable.
"France cannot afford to change direction all the time without taking serious risks," Chirac told the final meeting of his cabinet before the decisive vote.
To change direction now would lead the country into "confusion and weakness", Chirac was quoted as saying by government spokesman Alain Lamassoure.
The president urged centre-right ministers to explain to voters that "in the next five years, France must be governed in a modern, coherent and determined way".
But Socialist Party leader Lionel Jospin, the left's candidate for prime minister, urged Chirac to brace for a period of power-sharing with a leftist alliance.
Cohabitation, as the French refer to power-sharing, "shows respect for what the people have decided," Jospin said.
It "is nothing but an attitude, a type of behaviour, a spirit of responsibility towards one's country," he told Radio Luxembourg.

The left-wing opposition outpolled the centre-right coalition by more than four points in last Sunday's first round of voting and polling firms said it was on course for a narrow majority if the pattern were repeated in Sunday's runoff.

Chirac told his cabinet that the work done by outgoing Prime Minister Alain Juppe, who has announced he will resign whatever the election result, had enabled the country to face the next stage of its development "in good conditions".
Seeking to lure back disenchanted voters, Chirac had said in a brief televised message on Tuesday that he had heard their message but urged them not to return to "the socialist ideas of yesteryear".
But most commentators dismissed his appeal as too little too late, saying it had fallen short of the dramatic gesture needed to give his government a new lease on life.
"Is that all there is?" headlined the daily France-Soir over a picture of Chirac in a Superman costume.
"Chirac's unobtainable elan: Already braced for cohabitation," said the centre-left daily Liberation.
Only the pro-government Le Figaro touted Chirac's statement, saying he had breathed new life into the majority.
French presidents typically try to appear above everyday politics but Chirac was obliged to intervene as leader of the government's campaign after forcing Juppe to quit.
At stake for the president is a friendly parliament for the final five years of his seven-year presidential term.

His gamble of dissolving the National Assembly, with its strong centre-right majority, and holding an election nearly 10 months early to strengthen his hand as France heads into European monetary union, has already gone badly wrong.
"Let us take care not to compromise everything at the moment when we are reaping the first fruits of our efforts," the Gaullist president said in his televised speech.
But Communist Party leader Robert Hue, speaking on Radio Monte Carlo, said the "fruits" consisted of "continuing unemployment, economic uncertainty, difficulties and privatisations".
"The French people no longer want these fruits," he said.
